market_context: US/Canada audience; maternal identity and feeling overlooked during pregnancy.
title: When everything is about the baby and you miss people asking about you

seo.title: When everything is about the baby and you miss being asked about you
seo.meta_description: You can be excited about the baby and still feel invisible when every conversation revolves around pregnancy. Make room for your own life and identity too.
seo.search_intent: Support pregnant women who feel others have stopped showing interest in them as individuals.

excerpt: You can love and anticipate your baby while missing questions about your work, ideas, friendships, or simply how you are — not just how pregnancy is going.
content_html:
The baby can take over conversation long before birth. Relatives ask about size, purchases, names, and plans. Friends ask how pregnancy is going. Even gatherings that once had many subjects can start orbiting the same news.

You can be excited about your baby and still miss being interesting to other people as a whole person.

Feeling displaced does not mean you are competing with your baby

You are not asking for the baby to matter less. You are noticing that you still have work, friendships, humor, worries, ideas, and an inner life that did not vanish when pregnancy began.

Ask for the kind of attention you miss

People may believe pregnancy questions are the best way to show care and not realize how repetitive the topic has become. With someone close, you can say, “I love that you care, and I also miss talking with you about the rest of my life.”

Keep relationships where you do not have to perform “the pregnant person”

A meal, walk, or phone call where symptoms are not the opening question can feel surprisingly restorative. Protect those spaces and help create them by suggesting topics and activities that belonged to you before pregnancy.

Notice who can see you while also celebrating the baby

Pregnancy can reveal which relationships remain curious about you and which rely heavily on the life event of the moment. You do not have to end relationships over that, but you can move closer to people who still ask what you think, need, and care about.

Becoming a mother adds to your identity. It does not need to occupy every inch of it before the baby is even born.

faq.question: Is it selfish to want people to ask about me instead of only the baby?
faq.answer: No. Wanting interest, conversation, and recognition as a person is fully compatible with loving your baby.

faq.question: How can I say this without sounding accusatory?
faq.answer: Focus on what you miss: “I love that you ask about pregnancy, and I miss talking with you about other parts of my life too.”

faq.question: What if every conversation returns to pregnancy?
faq.answer: Suggest non-pregnancy activities and topics, and protect time with people who support other parts of your identity.
